demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal
Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: 'Talks or photos about snakes' is not clinically coherent as a trigger for PTSD centered on the unexpected death of a loved one unless the death involved snakes, which is not indicated. It appears trauma-unrelated and weakly connected to the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: 'I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened' implies perceived preventability and personal responsibility during the death event. That can occur, but it is not supported by the rest of the profile, which lacks any memory or trigger content suggesting direct involvement in the loved one's death.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships
issues.explanation: 'Starting new friendships or relationships' as an avoided strategy is a poor fit for a married 28-year-old male whose trauma is bereavement, and it is not well linked to the stated triggers/appraisals. It suggests interpersonal avoidance without supporting appraisals such as mistrust, fear of loss, or social threat.

vignette:
Marco, a 28-year-old prison guard living in a small Texas border town, had always considered himself steady-someone who could handle the pressure of the job without letting it follow him home. That changed fourteen months ago, when his younger brother, Daniel, was killed in a drive-by shooting outside a convenience store. Marco had been on shift that night, locked inside the unit, and by the time he got the call, Daniel was already gone. He had not been there to protect him, and that thought had taken root in his chest like something living.

In the weeks after the funeral, Marco began to notice that certain things would pull him back into that night with a force that felt physical. A news report about gang violence, even a brief mention on the radio, would leave his hands shaking. When a coworker mentioned losing a cousin to gunfire, Marco felt his mind go distant-the room around him seemed to become thin and unreal, as if he were watching himself from somewhere far away. He had come to believe that these moments proved something terrible about him: that he was no longer the person he used to be. He would think, I used to be a happy person, but now I am always miserable, and the certainty that he had no future would settle over him like a weight.

To cope, Marco started covering his face with his hands whenever a grief reminder appeared-an old photograph, a song Daniel had liked, a conversation about someone losing a loved one. He would press his palms against his eyes until the pressure drowned out the image. But the strategy never held. The more he hid, the more convinced he became that he had failed his brother, that he was weak, that he was broken beyond repair. And those appraisals, in turn, made the triggers feel more dangerous. He began scanning his environment for anything that could remind him of loss, and he found it everywhere-in a coworker's offhand comment, in a news headline scrolling across the breakroom TV. Each time, he felt the familiar detachment creep in, and he would think, See, you can't escape it. You'll never escape it.

At work, Marco started picking arguments with other guards over small things-a schedule change, a misplaced logbook. He did not understand why he did it, only that the flash of anger gave him a few minutes of relief from the hollow dread that sat under his ribs. But the arguments left him feeling worse afterward. He would replay the exchange and tell himself that he was becoming someone his brother would not recognize, someone angry and isolated and lost. That judgment made him more vigilant for the next trigger, more certain that the world was full of reminders waiting to ambush him. He had come to believe that his only choice was to stay ahead of them, even if that meant creating a crisis of his own.

He stopped going to family dinners where Daniel's name might come up. He told his wife that he was too tired to talk. The avoidance had become a kind of second job, and it was wearing him down. What finally brought Marco to the clinic was a morning when he had walked into the prison's common area and heard a newscast about a shooting in San Antonio. He had frozen, covered his face, and then, without knowing why, had yelled at a colleague who asked if he was okay. The look on the man's face-surprise, concern, pity-had stayed with Marco all day. That night, he told his wife that he could not keep living like this. He was afraid that if he did not get help, he would lose everything he had left, and he was terrified that there might be nothing left to save.
